catalog_quote: Ho does, however, have predictable stress assignment... light syllables are those that have CV or VC pattern. Heavy syllables include CVV (long vowels and diphthongs) and CVC. Superheavy syllables (CVVC) do not behave differently from heavy syllables for stress assignment. There are also extra-light syllables in Ho, consisting of just V... they are extra-metrical... Stress in Ho is organized in a trochaic pattern; a prominent syllable is followed by a weaker one. The domain of stress is the metrical foot... in simple CV.CV words, the first syllable is always more prominent. [ˈmu.ni] 'hermit' [ˈsa.du] 'holy man'... Exceptions to the basic rule occur when the second syllable is heavier than the first and it attracts greater relative prominence. sources.citation: Nottrott, A. 1882. Grammatik der Kolh-Sprache. Gütersloh: Bertelsmann. (archive.org grammatikderkolh00nottuoft, scanned text) — Chota Nagpur Kherwarian ('Kolh'), cited as a Ho stress source by Horo & Anderson 2021 Table 2
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Der Ton liegt meistens auf der ersten Silbe, selbst wenn diese die viertletzte ist. Ausgenommen davon sind die Formen des Infinitivs und die Worte, welche sich auf einen Diphtong endigen; diese haben den Ton auf der drittletzten Silbe.' (default initial stress even in 4-syllable words; infinitives and diphthong-final words stress the antepenult). Consistent with a left-edge/trochaic default; the exceptions are morpholexical rather than weight-based. 19th-c. missionary grammar and the languoid is Chota Nagpur 'Kolh' (Mundari/Ho area), so only weak corroboration.
